citation.title: Cluster-Robust Variance Estimation for Dyadic Data

standing_assumptions:
The article is Aronow, Samii and Assenova, ‘Cluster–Robust Variance Estimation for Dyadic Data’, Political Analysis 23:564–577 (2015). Printed page = PDF page + 563 (printed p. 566 is PDF p. 3). Everything quoted below and in the targets was read from the rendered page images (staged/pages/p-NN.png, checked against 200–300 dpi renderings of staged/main.pdf). Primes are transposes. The paper writes $\epsilon_d$ for the population residual and $e_d$ for the fitted (sample) residual; the two are different objects throughout.
(S1) Sampling and dyads, p. 566 (PDF p. 3): “Begin with a large population from which we take a random (i.i.d.) sample of units, with the sample members indexed by $i = 1, ..., N$ and grouped into $D = \binom{N}{2} = N(N-1)/2$ dyads. Pairs of unit indices within each dyad map to dyadic indices, $1, ..., D$, through the index function $d(i,j) = d(j,i)$, with an inverse correspondence $s(d(i,j)) = \{i,j\}$, and we assume no $d(i,i)$ type dyads.”
(S2) Regression and estimand, p. 566: “Consider a linear regression of $Y_{d(i,j)}$ on a $k$-length column vector of regressors $X_{d(i,j)}$ (which includes the constant): $$Y_{d(i,j)} = X'_{d(i,j)}\beta + \epsilon_{d(i,j)},$$ where $\beta$ is the slope that we would obtain if we could fit this model to the entire population, allowing for possible non-linearity in the true relationship between $\mathrm{E}[Y_{d(i,j)}|X_{d(i,j)}]$ and $X_{d(i,j)}$, and $\epsilon_{d(i,j)}$ is the corresponding population residual.$^3$ To lighten notation, for the remainder of the discussion we use $d = d(i,j)$.” Footnote 3, p. 566: “If $\mathrm{E}[Y_{d(i,j)}|X_{d(i,j)}]$ is non-linear in $X_{d(i,j)}$, the population residual will itself vary in $X_{d(i,j)}$, which undermines inference that assumes that $\epsilon_{d(i,j)}$ is independent of $X_{d(i,j)}$. The agnostic regression approach avoids such an assumption.”
(S3) Estimator, p. 566: “Define the sample data as $\mathbf{X} = (X_1 ... X_D)'$ and $Y = (Y_1 ... Y_D)'$. The ordinary least squares (OLS) estimator is $$\hat\beta = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}'Y,$$ with residual $e_d = Y_d - X'_d\hat\beta$.”
(S4) Dependence, boundedness and rank, p. 566: “Since the values of $Y_d$ and $X_d$ are determined by the characteristics of the units $i$ and $j$, $\epsilon_d$ and $\epsilon_{d'}$ for dyads containing either unit $i$ or $j$ are allowed to be correlated by construction. However, by random sampling of units, $\mathrm{Cov}(\epsilon_d, \epsilon_{d'}) = 0$ for all dyads that do not share a member. The number of pairwise dependencies between $i$ and $j$ for which $\mathrm{Cov}(\epsilon_d, \epsilon_{d'}) \ne 0$ is $O(N^3)$. Let the support for $X_d$ and $Y_d$ be bounded in a finite interval and assume the usual rank conditions on $\mathbf{X}$ (Chamberlain 1982; White 1984).”
(S5) Neighbouring dyads, p. 566 (repeated on p. 573): “$\mathcal{S}(d) = \{d' \ne d\} \cap \{d' : s(d) \cap s(d') \ne \emptyset\}$, the set of dyads other than $d$ that share a member from $d$.”
(S6) Repeated dyads, p. 567 (PDF p. 4): “Formally, suppose that for each dyad $d$ observations are indexed by $t = 1, ..., T(d)$, where the $T(d)$ values are fixed and finite. Let $(Y_{dt}, X'_{dt})$ represent the data for observation $t$ from dyad $d$, $$Y_d = \begin{pmatrix} Y_{d1} \\ \vdots \\ Y_{dT(d)} \end{pmatrix} \quad\text{and}\quad X_d = \begin{pmatrix} X'_{d1} \\ \vdots \\ X'_{dT(d)} \end{pmatrix},$$ and $Y = (Y'_1 \ldots Y'_d \ldots Y'_D)'$ and $\mathbf{X} = (X'_1 \ldots X'_d \ldots X'_D)'$, that is, the stacked $Y_d$ vectors and $X_d$ matrices, and let $\beta_r$ and $\hat\beta_r$ denote, respectively, the population slope and OLS estimator as defined above but now applied to the repeated dyads data.” In this case $X_d$ is a $T(d) \times k$ matrix and $e_d$, $\epsilon_d$ are $T(d)$-vectors.
(S7) Weighted observations, Appendix D, p. 575 (PDF p. 12): “Assume weighted directed dyad observations with weights finite and fixed; denote the weight for dyad $d$ as $w_d$. Define the sample data as $\mathbf{X} = (X'_1 ... X'_D)'$ and $Y = (Y_1 ... Y_D)'$ and the matrix of weights as $\mathbf{W} = \mathrm{diag}\{w_1, \ldots, w_D\}$. Then, the weighted least squares estimator is $$\hat\beta_w = (\mathbf{X}'WX)^{-1}\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{W}Y.$$” (In the display the $W$ and $X$ inside the inverse are set in italic, not bold; the meaning is $(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{-1}$.) The paper does not define $\beta_w$.
(S8) Simulation design, p. 569 (PDF p. 6): “We suppose that population values obey the following: $$Y_{d(i,j)t} = \beta_0 + \beta_1|X_i - X_j| + \underbrace{\alpha_i + \alpha_j + \nu_{d(i,j)t}}_{\epsilon_{d(i,j)t}}, \qquad (4)$$ where $Y_{d(i,j)t}$ is the $t$th observed outcome for the dyad that includes units $i$ and $j$, $X_i$, $X_j$, $\alpha_i$, $\alpha_j$, and $u_{d(i,j)t}$ are independent draws from standard normal distributions, and the compound error, $\epsilon_{d(i,j)t} = \alpha_i + \alpha_j + \nu_{d(i,j)t}$, is unobserved. In the cross-sectional case, we only observe one outcome per dyad, so $t = 1$ for all observations (i.e., the $t$ subscript is extraneous for the cross-sectional case). In the repeated observations case, we have two observations per dyad, so $t = 1, 2$ for all dyads. We fix $\beta_0 = 0$ and $\beta_1 = 1$. We use OLS to estimate $\hat\beta_0$ and $\hat\beta_1$.”
(S9) Reading used by the validators (the audit's formalization of S1–S4; not printed as such). Each unit carries a characteristic $U_i$, the $U_i$ are i.i.d., and $(X_{d(i,j)}, Y_{d(i,j)}) = f(U_i, U_j)$ for one symmetric measurable $f$, with $X_d \in \mathbb{R}^k$ and $Y_d \in \mathbb{R}$ bounded. Hence collections of dyads on disjoint sets of units are independent, and all dyads have the same marginal law. $Q = \mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d]$ is nonsingular (the ‘usual rank conditions’), $\beta = Q^{-1}\mathrm{E}[X_dY_d]$ is the population least-squares projection, $\epsilon_d = Y_d - X'_d\beta$, so that $\mathrm{E}[X_d\epsilon_d] = 0$; nothing makes $\mathrm{E}[\epsilon_d|\mathbf{X}] = 0$. The limit is $N \to \infty$. For repeated dyads the reading is $\beta_r = (\sum_d \mathrm{E}[X'_dX_d])^{-1}\sum_d \mathrm{E}[X'_dY_d]$ and $\epsilon_d = Y_d - X_d\beta_r$; for weights, $\beta_w = (\sum_d w_d\mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d])^{-1}\sum_d w_d\mathrm{E}[X_dY_d]$ and $\epsilon_d = Y_d - X'_d\beta_w$.
Scope of the list. Targets are the paper's formal results (Lemma 1, Propositions 1–2, Corollaries 1–2, the logistic estimator of Appendix E) and every confirmed error whose correction changes a mathematical statement, a formula or a proof step: P018-E001, E002, E003, E004, E005, E006, E007, N001, N003, N004, N006, N010. Two findings about the reported evidence rest on exact formal arguments and are targets for that formal content only: P018-E008 (the fitted random-effects benchmark has a covariance family that excludes the covariance of design (4)) and P018-E012 (‘an order of magnitude’ against the ratios of Table 1; the validator's evidence is itself a Lean proof). Not targets: P018-E009 (a mislabelled curve in SI Figure 4), E010 (sample counts), E011 (description of a regressor), E014 and E015 (wording and reference-list misprints), N008 (a cross-reference), which are findings about figures, data, reporting and bibliography with no mathematical statement to correct; P018-E013 and N002 (clarity notes); P018-N005 and N009 (not confirmed); P018-N007, N011, N012, N013 (out of scope). Of the headline claims, P018-H1 (Lemma 1, Proposition 1), H3 (Corollaries 1–2), H4 (Appendix E) and H5 (Proposition 2) are mathematical statements and are covered by P018-T26–T29, T14 and T16; H2 is the interpretive claim of valid inference under misspecification, whose formal content is T2, T4 and T8; H6–H10 are simulation and empirical claims.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 4 (pp. 569–570), Supporting Information p. 2 and the Conclusion (p. 572): the statements that design (4) with normal data ‘corresponds precisely to’ / ‘conforms exactly to’ the assumptions of the fitted two-way random effects model, as printed, with the model the replication archive fits
canonical_claim.location: pp. 569–570 (PDF pp. 6–7); Supporting Information p. 2; p. 572 (PDF p. 9); replication scripts 1 (line 86) and 2 (line 78)
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed, pp. 569–570: “In the supplementary information, we demonstrate comparisons between mixed-effects models and our “robust” estimator.$^6$ Specifically, we compare OLS with dyadic cluster robust standard errors to a two-way random effects model that incorporates normal random effects for each of the $N$ units (Gelman and Hill 2007). The data-generating process captured above (i.e., expression 4 with normal data) corresponds precisely to the assumptions of a two-way normal random effects model, and so it is no surprise that we find this model to be more efficient than OLS and to produce consistent standard errors. However, as discussed above, such models are sensitive to misspecification.”
As printed, Supporting Information p. 2: “Figure 2 and 3 show additional simulation results where we make comparisons to mixed effects models—specifically, to a two-way random effects model that incorporates random effects for each of $N$ units in the data. All random effects models were fit using the lmer package in R.” and “Given that the data generating process conforms exactly to the assumptions of a two-way random effects model, we obtain the straightforward result that the random effects estimates are both more efficient (the blue diamonds tend to be lower than the black ones) and the random effects standard errors are consistent.”
As printed, p. 572: “Our simulations show that a two-way (for cross-sectional data) random effects model can be considerably more efficient and provide reliable inference when the conditional mean is correctly specified.”
The model fitted (replication archive, as recorded by both validators): lmer(dY~dX + (1|dyad1) + (1|dyad2),data=dataUp), where dyad1 and dyad2 are the first and second unit of each dyad.
Formal reading of the printed correspondence claim for the reported simulations: there exist variance components $t_1, t_2, s\ge0$ such that the covariance matrix of the errors of design (4), $C = ZZ' + I$, equals the covariance matrix $t_1Z_1Z'_1 + t_2Z_2Z'_2 + sI$ of the fitted model (notation of P018-T5). For $N\ge3$ this is false (P018-T5 (c)).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Equation (4): (S8). $Z_1$, $Z_2$, $Z$, $C$ and the family $W(t_1,t_2,s)$: P018-T5. The corrected claim: P018-T6. Footnote 6 (p. 569) concerns spatial error lag models and is not part of the claim.
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed for P018-E008 (error, Moderate). The sentences are true of a random-effects model with one shared effect per unit, which is what the text describes; they are false of the model the archive fits and the figures report. The formal reading above is the validators' (‘the natural reading of the precise-correspondence claim is therefore false’). ‘More efficient’, ‘consistent standard errors’ and ‘reliable inference’ are claims about simulation output; they are quoted for the record and are not formal targets.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Lemma 1 (equations (1) and (2)), as printed, with its proof in Appendix A (equations (5) and (6))
canonical_claim.location: p. 566 (PDF p. 3), Lemma 1; p. 573 (PDF p. 10), Appendix A
canonical_claim.statement:

As $N	o\infty$, the asymptotic distribution of $\sqrt N(\hat eta -  eta)$ has mean zero and variance $$V =  rac{N}{D^2}\mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d]^{-1}\mathrm{Var}\Big[\sum_{d=1}^{D}X_d\epsilon_d\Big]\mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d]^{-1}, \qquad (1)$$ with $$\mathrm{Var}\Big[\sum_{d=1}^{D}X_d\epsilon_d\Big] = \sum_{d=1}^{D}\Bigg(\underbrace{\mathrm{E}\{X_dX'_d\mathrm{Var}[\epsilon_d|\mathbf{X}]\}}_{A} + \underbrace{\sum_{d'\in\mathcal{S}(d)\,\mathrm{E}}\{X_dX'_{d'}\mathrm{Cov}[\epsilon_d,\epsilon_{d'}|\mathbf{X}]\}}_{B}\Bigg), \qquad (2)$$ where $\mathcal{S}(d) = \{d'

e\emptyset\}$, the set of dyads other than $d$ that share a member from $d$.” (In (2) the letter $\mathrm{E}$ of term $B$ is printed inside the summation subscript; see P018-T21.)
Text after the lemma (p. 566): “$A$ is the dyad-specific contribution to the variance, and $B$ is the contribution due to inclusion of common units in multiple dyads. Note that these features of the distribution of $\sqrt N(\hat eta -  eta)$ establish the consistency of $\hat eta$ as well, which is not surprising given standard results for the consistency of OLS coefficients on dependent data (White 1984).”
Hypotheses attached: the setting (S1)–(S5): i.i.d. sample of units, all $ inom N2$ dyads, $ eta$ the population slope allowing a non-linear conditional mean, $X_d$ and $Y_d$ with support bounded in a finite interval, ‘the usual rank conditions on $\mathbf{X}$’.
Proof as printed (Appendix A, p. 573): “Proof. We have $$\sqrt N(\hat eta -  eta) = \Big[ rac1D\sum_{d=1}^{D}X_dX'_d\Big]^{-1} rac{\sqrt N}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D}X_d\epsilon_d.$$ Take $[(1/D)\sum_{d=1}^{D}X_dX'_d]^{-1}$ first. By continuity of the inverse, the finite support of $X_d$ and $e_d$, $\mathbf{X}$ full rank, and the fact that the sum of dependent terms in this sum is $O(D^{3/2})$ (Lehmann 1999, Equation (2.8.4)), we have that $$\Big[ rac1D\sum_{d=1}^{D}X_dX'_d\Big]^{-1}\overset{p}{	o}\mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d]^{-1}.$$ By Slutsky's theorem, $\sqrt N(\hat eta -  eta)$ has the same asymptotic distribution as $\mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d]^{-1} rac{\sqrt N}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D}X_d\epsilon_d$, which has mean zero and variance, $$V =  rac{N}{D^2}\mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d]^{-1}\mathrm{Var}\Big[\sum_{d=1}^{D}X_d\epsilon_d\Big]\mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d]^{-1}. \qquad (5)$$ Then, $$\mathrm{Var}\Big[\sum_{d=1}^{D}X_d\epsilon_d\Big] = \sum_{d=1}^{D}\sum_{d'=1}^{D}\mathrm{Cov}[X_d\epsilon_d, X_{d'}\epsilon_{d'}] = \sum_{d=1}^{D}\sum_{d'=1}^{D}\mathrm{E}\{X_dX'_{d'}\mathrm{Cov}[\epsilon_d,\epsilon_{d'}|\mathbf{X}]\} = \sum_{d=1}^{D}\Bigg(\underbrace{\mathrm{E}\{X_dX'_d\mathrm{Var}[\epsilon_d|\mathbf{X}]\}}_{A} + \underbrace{\sum_{d'\in\mathcal{S}(d)}\mathrm{E}\{X_dX'_{d'}\mathrm{Cov}[\epsilon_d,\epsilon_{d'}|\mathbf{X}]\}}_{B}\Bigg), \qquad (6)$$ where $\mathcal{S}(d) = \{d'
e d\}\cap\{d' : s(d)\cap s(d')
e\emptyset\}$, the set of dyads other than $d$ that share a member from $d$.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Setting and notation: (S1)–(S5), (S9). $\mathbf{X} = (X_1 ... X_D)'$ is the whole sample design, so the conditioning in (2) and (6) is on all regressors. $V$ depends on $N$ through $N/D^2$ and the variance of the score sum; ‘the asymptotic distribution has variance $V$’ is read as: the limiting covariance of $\sqrt N(\hat\beta - \beta)$ is $\lim_NV$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact finite-population statements in the lemma and its proof. (F1) The least-squares identity (first display of Appendix A), valid on samples with $\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}$ nonsingular because $Y_d = X'_d\beta + \epsilon_d$: $\sqrt N(\hat\beta - \beta) = [D^{-1}\sum_dX_dX'_d]^{-1}(\sqrt N/D)\sum_dX_d\epsilon_d$. True. (F2) The count behind ‘the sum of dependent terms in this sum is $O(D^{3/2})$’: each dyad shares a member with exactly $2(N-2)$ other dyads, so there are $D\cdot2(N-2) = N(N-1)(N-2)$ ordered pairs of distinct dyads with a common member, and each entry of $D^{-1}\sum_dX_dX'_d$ has variance $O(1/N)$ for bounded $X_d$. True (held up by both readers). (F3) The first equality of (6), $\mathrm{Var}[\sum_dX_d\epsilon_d] = \sum_d\sum_{d'}\mathrm{Cov}[X_d\epsilon_d, X_{d'}\epsilon_{d'}]$. True. (F4) The second and third equalities of (6), and equation (2). False in general under the paper's setting: exact counterexample P018-T1; corrected identity P018-T2. (F5) Equation (1)/(5) is the exact covariance of $Q^{-1}(\sqrt N/D)\sum_dX_d\epsilon_d$, $Q = \mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d]$, for every $N$. True. The lemma states a mean and a variance of ‘the asymptotic distribution’ and no limit law; the central limit theorem that gives one under (S9) is P018-T8 (i).
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed for P018-E001 (error, Moderate), and with Proposition 1 the paper's headline result P018-H1. What stands: equation (1) with the actual (unconditional) variance of the score sum, the least-squares identity, the convergence of the Gram matrix; both fresh readers and both validators agree. What falls: equation (2) and the last two lines of (6) when the conditional mean is non-linear, the case the paper stresses. Other confirmed points on this passage: the misplaced $\mathrm{E}$ in (2) (P018-N001, P018-T21); ‘finite support of $X_d$ and $e_d$’ in Appendix A is loose wording for bounded support (P018-N002, a clarity note, not a target); the missing non-degeneracy condition for inference (P018-E002, P018-T7, P018-T8).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 1 (equation (3)), as printed, with its proof in Appendix B
canonical_claim.location: p. 567 (PDF p. 4), Proposition 1; pp. 573–574 (PDF pp. 10–11), Appendix B
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed (p. 567): “Proposition 1. Define the variance estimator $$\hat V = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\sum_{d=1}^{D}\Big(X_dX'_de_d^2 + \sum_{d'\in\mathcal{S}(d)}X_dX'_{d'}e_de_{d'}\Big)(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}. \qquad (3)$$ Under the conditions of Lemma 1 and if $X_{\mathrm{d}}$ and $e_d$ have bounded support with nonzero second moments and cross-moments, then as $N	o\infty$, $$N\hat V - V\overset{p}{	o}0.$$”
Text after the proposition (p. 567): “The proposition indicates that $\hat V$ provides a consistent estimator to characterize the true asymptotic sampling distribution of the regression coefficients, $\hat eta$. Standard error estimates for $\hat eta$ are obtained from the square roots of the diagonals of $\hat V$. The assumption of bounded support for $X_d$ and $e_d$ merely rules out situations that are unlikely to arise in real-world data anyway (e.g., where the mass of the data pushes out toward infinity as $N$ grows).”
Proof as printed (Appendix B, pp. 573–574): “Proof. By Chebyshev's inequality, two conditions are sufficient for $N\hat V - V\overset{p}{	o}0$ as $N	o\infty$: (i) $\mathrm{E}[\hat V - V]	o0$ and (ii) $\mathrm{Var}[N\hat V - V] = \mathrm{Var}[N\hat V]	o0$ (Lehmann 1999, Theorem 2.1.1). For (i), consider the interior (meat) of $\hat V$: $$\hat\Sigma = \sum_{d=1}^{D}\Big(X_dX'_de_d^2 + \sum_{d'\in\mathcal{S}(d)}X_dX'_{d'}e_de_{d'}\Big)$$ and the corresponding term for $V$: $$\Sigma = \sum_{d=1}^{D}\Big(\mathrm{E}\{X_dX'_d\mathrm{Var}[\epsilon_d|\mathbf{X}]\} + \sum_{d'\in\mathcal{S}(d)}\mathrm{E}\{X_dX'_{d'}\mathrm{Cov}[\epsilon_d,\epsilon_{d'}|\mathbf{X}]\}\Big).$$ We have $$\mathrm{E}[\hat\Sigma] = \sum_{d=1}^{D}\Big(\mathrm{E}\{X_dX'_d\mathrm{E}[e_d^2|\mathbf{X}]\} + \sum_{d'\in\mathcal{S}(d)}\mathrm{E}\{X_dX'_{d'}\mathrm{E}[e_de_{d'}|\mathbf{X}]\}\Big)	o\Sigma$$ by consistency of $\hat eta$, an implication of Lemma 1. Lemma 1 also established that $(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}/D)^{-1}\overset{p}{	o}\mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d]^{-1}$, while boundedness of $X_d$ implies uniform boundedness of $\mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d]^{-1}$. Taking these elements together, uniform continuity implies $\mathrm{E}[\hat V - V]	o0$ (cf. White 1980a, Theorem 1). For (ii), we follow the strategy of Lehmann (1999, Section 2.8), which requires showing that growth of covariance contributions due to dependent units is bounded in $N$. Begin by rewriting $N\hat V$ as $$N\hat V = N(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}/D)^{-1}\Big(D^{-2}\sum_d\sum_{d'}I_{d,d'}X_dX'_{d'}e_de_{d'}\Big)(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}/D)^{-1},$$ where $I_{d,d'}$ is an indicator function denoting a pair of dyads $d$ and $d'$ that share a member, as defined above. We have established that $(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}/D)^{-1}$ converges in probability to a finite limit, $E[X_dX_d']^{-1}$, so we can treat this as $O(1)$. Given bounded support, $\mathrm{Var}[N\hat V]$ is of the same order as $$\Omega = N^2D^{-4}\mathrm{Var}\Big[\sum_d\sum_{d'}I_{d,d'}X_dX'_{d'}e_de_{d'}\Big] = N^2D^{-4}\sum_d\sum_{d'}\sum_{d''}\sum_{d'''}\mathrm{Cov} ig(I_{d,d'}X_dX'_{d'}e_de_{d'},\ I_{d'',d'''}X_{d''}X'_{d'''}e_{d''}e_{d'''} ig).$$ To show $\mathrm{Var}[N\hat V]	o0$, it is sufficient to establish that $\Omega$ is at most $O(N^{-1})$. canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Lemma 1 and $V$ of equation (1): P018-T26. Setting: (S1)–(S5), (S9). $e_d = Y_d - X'_d\hat\beta$ is the fitted residual. In the first line of the proposition's hypothesis the subscript of $X_{\mathrm{d}}$ is printed upright (P018-N002, a clarity note). The symbols $\Omega$ and $Q$ of Appendix B (a scalar order bound and a number of quadruples) are not the $\Omega$ and $Q$ of other targets.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact finite statements in the proposition and its printed proof. (F1) The rewriting $N\hat V = N(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}/D)^{-1}\big(D^{-2}\sum_d\sum_{d'}I_{d,d'}X_dX'_{d'}e_de_{d'}\big)(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}/D)^{-1}$, with $I_{d,d'} = 1$ exactly when $s(d)\cap s(d')\ne\emptyset$ (including $d = d'$). True. (F2) The Chebyshev step as printed, with the mean condition (i) $\mathrm{E}[\hat V - V]\to0$. False as a sufficiency claim and false of the estimator in an admissible model: P018-T3 (d), (e); corrected form P018-T4. (F3) ‘$\mathrm{E}[\hat\Sigma]\to\Sigma$’ without normalization. False: P018-T3 (c). (F4) The claim that nonzero covariances between products $e_de_{d'}$ and $e_{d''}e_{d'''}$ occur only in the six listed shared-unit cases. False for fitted residuals: P018-T3 (g). For population residuals the corresponding count is true and is P018-T4 (L4). (F5) The treatment of $(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}/D)^{-1}$ as $O(1)$ inside an expectation and a variance. Not justified by convergence in probability: P018-T3 (h), (i), P018-T19. (F6) $\Sigma$ is defined with conditional variances and covariances: P018-T1, P018-T2.
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed for P018-E006 (error, Moderate), and with Lemma 1 the paper's headline result P018-H1. No failure of the conclusion $N\hat V - V\overset{p}{\to}0$ is established: with $V$ defined through equation (1) it holds under the paper's own setting by the replacement argument P018-T4. The printed proof does not establish it. The sentence on standard errors after the proposition is the subject of P018-N003 (P018-T17, P018-T18) and P018-E002 (P018-T7, P018-T8).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Corollary 1 (repeated dyads), as printed, with the display for $V_r$
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed (pp. 567–568): “Corollary 1. For the repeated dyads case, assume the same conditions as in Proposition 1 and consider the following variance estimator: $$\hat V_r = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}\sum_{d=1}^{D}\Big(X'_de_de'_dX_d + \sum_{d'\in\mathcal{S}(d)}X'_de_de'_{d'}X_{d'}\Big)(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X})^{-1}.$$ Then, as $N\to\infty$, $$N\mathrm{Var}[\hat\beta_r - \beta_r] - V_r\overset{p}{\to}0,$$ and $$N\hat V_r - V_r\overset{p}{\to}0,$$ where $$V_r = \frac{N}{\big[\sum_{d=1}^{D}T(d)\big]^2}\mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d]^{-1}\mathrm{E}\Big(\mathrm{E}[X'_d\mathrm{Cov}[\epsilon_d|\mathbf{X}]X_d] + \sum_{d'\in\mathcal{S}(d)}\mathrm{E}[X'_d\mathrm{Cov}[\epsilon_d,\epsilon_{d'}|\mathbf{X}]X_{d'}]\Big)\mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d]^{-1}.$$”
Hypotheses attached: the repeated-dyads setting (S6), with the $T(d)$ ‘fixed and finite’; ‘the same conditions as in Proposition 1’ (P018-T27), i.e. (S1)–(S5) and bounded support of $X_d$ and $e_d$ with nonzero second moments and cross-moments.
Remark printed after the corollary (p. 568): “First, our analysis of the repeated observations case takes the $T(d)$ values to be fixed and finite and demonstrates consistency as $N$ grows. [...] Under fixed $N$ and growing $T(d)$ further assumptions would be required for consistency, such as serial correlation of fixed order or, more generally, strong mixing over time.”
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Repeated setting: (S6); $X_d$ is $T(d)\times k$, $e_d$ and $\epsilon_d$ are $T(d)$-vectors, $\mathrm{Cov}[\epsilon_d|\mathbf{X}]$ a $T(d)\times T(d)$ matrix, $\mathrm{Cov}[\epsilon_d,\epsilon_{d'}|\mathbf{X}]$ a $T(d)\times T(d')$ matrix. $\beta_r$, $\hat\beta_r$: (S6), read as in (S9). $\mathcal{S}(d)$: (S5). The paper gives no proof of the corollary (‘The results above translate straightforwardly to the repeated dyads setting’, p. 567).
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: The corollary has no printed proof. The exact finite statements on which a proof of its corrected form rests are: the linearization identity $\sqrt N(\hat\beta_r - \beta_r) = (\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}/L)^{-1}(\sqrt N/L)\sum_dX'_d\epsilon_d$, $L = \sum_dT(d)$, and the exact covariance $V_r = (N/L^2)H_r^{-1}\Omega_rH_r^{-1}$ of its linear approximation (P018-T12); the dimension count that $X'_dX_d$ is $k\times k$ and $X_dX'_d$ is $T(d)\times T(d)$ (P018-T11 (e)); the count and bounds L1–L6 of P018-T4 applied to the block scores $X'_d\epsilon_d$; and the algebraic decomposition of $\hat V_r$ (Proposition 2, P018-T16).
canonical_claim.note: Headline result P018-H3 (with Corollary 2), asymptotic. As printed the statement cannot be formalized faithfully as a true theorem: the display for $V_r$ has an outer expectation where the sum over dyads belongs and bread matrices $\mathrm{E}[X_dX'_d]^{-1}$ of the wrong dimension (P018-E004, Minor: counterexample P018-T11, corrected target P018-T12); its middle factor uses conditional covariances (P018-E001: P018-T1, P018-T2); the first conclusion asserts convergence of a finite-sample variance that need not exist (P018-N004: P018-T19, P018-T20); and ‘fixed and finite’ must be read as a uniform bound (P018-E003: P018-T9, P018-T10). The estimator $\hat V_r$ itself is as intended and is what the authors' code computes. The intended, corrected corollary is P018-T10 (C1) with the target of P018-T12; this entry fixes the printed text for comparison. The two sentences on fixed $N$ and growing $T(d)$ are the subject of P018-N005 (not confirmed).
